moves.spoken: We open with the king's pawn and Black declares the French.
We take the full center with the d-pawn — the invitation the French always accepts.
Black strikes at our center with d5. This is the defining tension of the French: the pawn on e4 has to decide its fate.
We choose the Advance — lock the chain and take the space. The pawn on e5 cramps Black's kingside and hands us a long-term spatial edge; the whole game will be about who breaks the chain first.
teaches: Advance = space + a fixed pawn chain

moves.spoken: Instead of the near-universal c5, Black tries the rare b6, planning to reroute the light-squared bishop to a6 and trade off the French's famously bad bishop before it gets buried behind the chain.
Worth being clear: almost everyone meets the Advance with c5, hitting the base of the chain. b6 is a comparatively rare sideline.
The whole point of b6 is that bishop-to-a6 trade. Against it there's no reason to hurry — we just develop and let Black spend the tempi.
teaches: answer a slow plan with fast development

moves.spoken: Here's the clever touch: the quiet c3 first. It looks like nothing, but it lays a trap for the immediate a6 trade — and the reason is worth pausing on.
Black finds the correct reply, tucking the queen to d7 rather than grabbing the trade at once.

This is why the immediate a6 fails: after the bishops come off, the knight recaptures on a6, and then a queen check on a4 skewers the loose knight and simply wins it. So the trade has to be prepared first.
teaches: Qa4 skewer on the a6 knight

moves.spoken: That's what the queen on d7 is for — it covers the a4-to-e8 diagonal, so once the bishop reaches a6 the Qa4 trick no longer bites and the trade becomes safe.
teaches: guarding the diagonal to enable the trade

moves.spoken: We develop the bishop to d3, its best diagonal in the Advance — aimed straight at Black's kingside where our space advantage will tell.
Black carries out the plan with the bishop to a6, offering to swap off the light-squared bishops.

The key decision — and the move most players get wrong. Not the natural Nf3 but the knight to e2, because it leaves the f-pawn unobstructed. That is the whole strategic key to the Advance: once we castle we want the thematic f4-f5 break to storm the kingside, and a knight on f3 would block it. From here the plan writes itself. Black concedes the light-squared bishops but loses tempi doing it; when he lunges with h5 he only hands us a weak square on g5 that we'd occupy with the dark-squared bishop — and we don't rush h4 ourselves, we wait for Black to push it and then freeze it with h3, since a pawn that comes to h4 becomes a target once our knight reroutes to g3 and later f3. On the queenside we play the advanced-French idea a3 and b4 to force the c-pawn to commit, prying open the c-file to double rooks, with a prophylactic h3 to deny Ng4. Then the classic finish: having won the queenside, we swing the queen to the kingside and play on both wings at once, where Black is most exposed.
teaches: Ne2 keeps the f-pawn free for f4
provoke h4 then fix it with h3
plans: double on the c-file, then attack the king

moves.spoken: A clean conversion — the passed pawn ran home with a square of luft always in reserve for our own king.
To recap the theory: b6 is a viable, well-known French sideline, though the mainstream choice stays c5.
Against the normal c5 our intended route was the knight-to-f3 line.
That's the c5 mainline, meeting it by developing the knight to f3 and supporting the chain.
After the exchange on d4 we recapture with the bishop to d3 and reach the same attacking setup — a line an earlier speedrun already walked through.

The fullest summary: c3 is clever precisely because an immediate a6 drops a piece to Qa4, so Qd7 is the standard reply; then bishop to d3, bishop to a6, knight to e2, all preparing the f4 break with the knight often swinging to g3. And on the h5 idea — don't answer with h4 of your own. If Black shoves the pawn to h4 it becomes a weakness we attack once the knight reaches f3, so it's better to wait and fix it with h3 than to create weaknesses yourself.
teaches: wait-and-fix beats committing your own h-pawn
